newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani cabinet approves anti-corruption bill.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani cabinet approves anti-corruption bill.

text.p: Pakistan's caretaker cabinet approved on Thursday a draft bill aimed at cracking down on corruption in high places, a senior government official said.

The proposed law would allow the federal ombudsman to start proceedings against politicians, bureaucrats and some members of the police and armed forces -- but not the president -- on corruption complaints submitted by the public.
"If a prima facie case is found, the ombudsman will refer the case to a high court," said the official, who asked not to be named.
The bill excludes the president, who has constitutional protection from criminal proceedings while in office.
The official said the bill would also expose military officers in civilian jobs to possible prosecution, but not all military officers, as proposed in the original draft.
He said the draft bill would be implemented by a presidential ordinance within three days.
He said the original draft had been amended to spare those who repaid money they had embezzled from going to jail.

Benazir Bhutto's ousted government and the main opposition Pakistan Muslim League placed separate anti-corruption bills before the National Assembly (lower house) before President Farooq Leghari dissolved it on November 5.
Bhutto's bill had included the president among those against whom corruption charges could be pursued.

When Leghari dismissed Bhutto's government, he said it had been paralysed by corruption, nepotism and misrule. Leghari had previously urged the former government and opposition to agree to set up parliamentary committees to fight corruption.

The caretaker government, which has a 90-day mandate to prepare for elections on February 3, has said it is preparing undisclosed charges against Bhutto and her husband, Asif Ali Zardari, who was investment minister in his wife's cabinet.
